title: Voices in the Narrative
text:
Many nineteenth-century novelists relied on an omniscient narrator who could enter the minds of several characters at once. Jane Austen, however, often blended the narrator's voice with the thoughts of her heroines, so that the reader hears a character's opinions without any explicit announcement. This technique, known as free indirect discourse, allows irony to emerge gradually.

The effect is subtle. A reader may feel sympathy for a character one moment and then notice, through a carefully chosen adjective, that the narrator quietly disagrees. Such shifts reward attentive readers, who must decide for themselves where sincerity ends and self-deception begins.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what kind of narrator could enter the minds of several characters at once?
According to the second paragraph, how can a reader notice that the narrator disagrees with a character?
options: Through a direct statement in dialogue
Through a footnote added by the editor

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about the effect of this technique on readers?
options: It requires readers to interpret the text actively
It makes the text simpler to follow
It removes the need for irony
It prevents readers from sympathizing with characters

questions.text: Why might the author describe the effect of the technique as 'subtle'?
options: Because it appears only in the final chapter
Because its effects build gradually and are easy to miss
Because it is found exclusively in poetry

vocabulary.definition: knowing everything, especially about characters' thoughts in a story
a contrast between what is said or expected and what is actually meant
a feeling of understanding and sharing another person's feelings

paragraph_translations: Wielu powieściopisarzy XIX wieku polegało na narratorze wszechwiedzącym, który mógł jednocześnie wejść w umysły kilku bohaterów. Jane Austen jednak często łączyła głos narratora z myślami swoich bohaterek, tak że czytelnik słyszy opinie postaci bez wyraźnej zapowiedzi. Ta technika, znana jako swobodna mowa pośrednia, pozwala ironii stopniowo się ujawniać.

Efekt jest subtelny. Czytelnik może w jednej chwili współczuć bohaterowi, a potem zauważyć, dzięki starannie dobranemu przymiotnikowi, że narrator po cichu się z nim nie zgadza. Takie przesunięcia nagradzają uważnych czytelników, którzy sami muszą zdecydować, gdzie kończy się szczerość, a zaczyna samooszukiwanie się.
